item.title: Arkansas Governor to appoint temporary replacement for recovering Justice Barbara Webb

item.content:encoded:
Above: Justice Barbara Webb. Photo courtesy of Arkansas Judiciary.

Arkansas Supreme Court Chief Justice Karen Baker has formally requested that Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders appoint a temporary special justice to fill the seat of Associate Justice Barbara Webb, of Benton, Arkansas, who is recovering from a head injury.

The request, made in a letter on Monday, comes as Webb’s family anticipates her potential return for the court’s fall term but seeks a temporary replacement to ensure the court remains at its full constitutional capacity during her recovery. Read more below.




In May, Justice Webb sustained a head injury following a fall at her home while doing laundry late in the evening, according to her husband Doyle Webb. She has since been undergoing treatment for the injury at a medical facility in Houston, Texas.

According to her husband, Doyle Webb, she is scheduled to return to Little Rock to undergo one additional surgery at UAMS, which will be followed by an unspecified recovery period. Doyle Webb stated that he advised Chief Justice Baker of his wife’s condition, noting that while Justice Webb anticipates returning to her duties in time for the Supreme Court’s fall term, they requested a temporary replacement in the event her recovery requires more time than currently expected.

In her letter to Governor Sanders on Monday, August 10, 2026, Chief Justice Baker formally certified that Justice Webb is temporarily unable to perform her judicial duties. Rather than requesting that a separate special justice be appointed for each individual case during her absence, Baker requested the appointment of a single temporary special justice who can handle all of Webb’s duties until she is able to resume them.

Under Amendment 80, Section 13(A) of the Arkansas Constitution, if a Supreme Court Justice is temporarily unable to serve, the Chief Justice certifies this to the Governor, who then has 30 days to commission a Special Justice. The temporary appointment will expire as soon as Webb notifies the Supreme Court that she is ready and able to return.

Under state constitutional requirements, the Arkansas Supreme Court must be composed of seven justices to function at full capacity. The transition to a temporary replacement ensures that the court will avoid potential delays or split decisions in upcoming cases during the transition period.

Benton Mayor Tom Farmer has secured official endorsements from the city’s police and fire unions as he campaigns for a third term in the upcoming Nov. 3 election. The endorsements come in a period of public safety expansion, including new facilities, equipment upgrades, and increased staffing levels across both departments. Read more below.




Farmer announced endorsements from the Fraternal Order of Police of the Benton Police Department and Fire Local 2765 of the Benton Fire Department. In a campaign release, the mayor expressed gratitude for the support, emphasizing the critical role both organizations play in protecting city residents.

During his tenure, which began in 2019, the Benton Police Department has grown to include 91 certified personnel and 10 civilian employees. To accommodate this growth, the police department relocated to the former City Hall building, while City Hall operations were moved to a former school building on River Street. The city has also continued to replace and expand its fleet of police vehicles.

A central focus of Farmer’s administration has been school safety. The city has successfully placed a certified school resource officer on every Benton school campus, as well as one at the Saline County Career Technical Campus.

The Benton Fire Department has similarly expanded, now employing 71 personnel. This includes the addition of nine firefighters to staff a newly constructed fire station located at Interstate 30 exit 114. The station, built on land donated by local resident Dan Moudy, was strategically placed to serve the growing area, which now houses the new Mountain View elementary and middle schools. Additionally, the city procured a new fire truck for Station 6 and anticipates the delivery of a new ladder truck by the end of August.

Despite the infrastructure renovations and personnel additions, Farmer noted that city tax and millage rates have remained unchanged for the past eight years. According to the mayor, all capital expenditures, equipment purchases, and safety improvements were achieved without implementing any new taxes on residents.

item.content:encoded:
See candidates for Federal, State & County offices at www.mysaline.com/2026-elections. The General Election is November 3, 2026. 

Municipal candidates are finished filing to run for office, and the August 5th deadline has passed. Several offices drew challengers, particularly in the City of Benton. However there are 41 candidates who managed to file unopposed, and they have all but won the election already.

Correction 08/07/26: There was a candidate mistakenly listed for Alexander City Council Ward 3, Position 2, but it’s a Shannon Hills candidate. They are edited and highlighted below.

Read more below.




In summary, while there are 41 unopposed candidates, every municipality drew challengers in one or more races, except one.

Alexander offices drew challengers in two City Council races and the Mayor race.  Two candidates are looking to replace Juanita Wilson in Ward 4, Position 2. She was recently arrested for allegedly committing forgery on the job. Lastly, former Mayor Paul Mitchell hopes to replace his replacement, the current Mayor, Crystal Herrmann.

In Bauxite, all City Council positions are unopposed, but former Bauxite Police Chief and 2019 lottery winner Jamie Barlow, III will challenger one-term Mayor Eddie Jones who co-owns Rock Island General Store.

In Benton, Council members Frank Baptist, Chad Slaughter, Steve Lee and Mayor Tom Farmer each have two challengers. Council member Ann Spencer-Cole has one challenger.

Marketer Greg White and mortgage agent Preston Madison seek Baptist’s Ward 1, Position 1 seat. Master Plumber Quinn Marshall seeks Spencer-Cole’s seat in Ward 2, Position 1.

Jana Hogue, Wealth Strategist Jana Hogue, along with Systems Administrator Bret Stracener each look to capture the Ward 3, Position 1 seat. Slaughter only recently captured it himself, filling the remaining term left by the sudden passing of Bill Donnor.

Economic development leader Lamont Cornwell, along with Kerry Tebbe, will run for Ward 5, Position 1 against Lee. Veteran Don White and roofer Jacob Wear both seek the office of Mayor, against two-term Tom Farmer, the former coach and transportation director.

Bryant provided a couple of challengers. Amy Edwards, who currently serves on the Bryant Planning Commission filed for Council member Jack Moseley’s seat in Ward 4, Position 1. Mayor Chris Treat is challenged by Council member and laser maker Walter Burgess, co-owner of Power Technology Inc.

Haskell Mayor Clyde Crookham is challenged by Ray Garner, co-owner of Grounds and Grace Coffee, as well as Dallas Wright, a current Council member and Saline County employee.

In Shannon Hills, Lela Chism challenges Council member Mendy Barnes, and Shawn Andersyn challenges Council member Mary Guinn. In Traskwood, everyone is unopposed.
